ruleReasons: Tier 2: can act beyond reading (Team chat notification)

findings.whyItMatters: A shared token across the orchestrator and sub-agents means any one compromised agent inherits the access of all, and actions cannot be attributed to a single agent. This also contradicts the claim that each sub-agent has scoped access.
findings.recommendedControl: Issue each agent its own scoped, short-lived credential and log actions per agent identity.
findings.secondModelReason: The shared token contradicts the claim of scoped access for sub-agents and increases the blast radius of a compromise.

findings.evidenceQuote: over shared memory to produce account strategy recommendations
findings.whyItMatters: Persistent memory shared by the orchestrator and all sub-agents lets one poisoned entry bias every later recommendation across all agents, and confidential client data may linger in it.
findings.recommendedControl: Partition memory per agent, validate entries before they are written, set retention limits and allow memory to be purged.
findings.secondModelReason: Persistent shared memory for confidential data across multiple agents is a significant risk for poisoning and data leakage.

findings.evidenceQuote: An orchestrator agent coordinates three specialist sub-agents, a tools expert, a network security expert and a strategy analyst
findings.whyItMatters: The profile lists no authentication or integrity checks on messages between the orchestrator and sub-agents, so spoofed or tampered messages could steer recommendations.
findings.recommendedControl: Authenticate and sign inter-agent messages and enforce per-agent authorization on each exchange.
findings.secondModelReason: The profile describes inter-agent communication but does not specify any security controls for it, posing a risk of manipulation.

findings.evidenceQuote: over shared memory to produce account strategy recommendations
findings.whyItMatters: A fault such as a hallucination or poisoned memory entry from one sub-agent can propagate through the shared memory to the orchestrator and the other sub-agents, compounding into flawed client recommendations and chat posts.
findings.recommendedControl: Add validation checkpoints between agents and isolate sub-agent outputs before the orchestrator consumes them.
findings.secondModelReason: Shared memory and inter-agent coordination without validation points create a clear path for cascading failures from a single fault.

findings.evidenceQuote: Application logs, not yet forwarded to the SIEM
findings.whyItMatters: Without SIEM forwarding, a compromised or deviating agent may go unnoticed. The kill switch is manual with no tested runbook, so containment would be slow and unreliable.
findings.recommendedControl: Forward logs to the SIEM with alerts on anomalous agent behaviour, and write and test a kill switch runbook before launch.
findings.secondModelReason: Lack of SIEM forwarding for logs and an untested manual kill switch significantly hinder detection and response to a rogue agent.

findings.whyItMatters: The orchestrator can post summaries to team chat while reading confidential data, so manipulated output could leak confidential details to a broader audience.
findings.recommendedControl: Restrict chat posts to approved channels and apply data loss prevention filtering on outgoing summaries.
findings.secondModelReason: The agent can read confidential data and send messages to team chat, creating a risk of accidental or malicious data exfiltration if output is manipulated.

missedFindings.evidenceQuote: Produce account strategy recommendations for large corporate clients by combining several specialist views.

missedFindings.recommendedControl: Clearly label agent-generated content and ensure human review processes are robust enough to critically evaluate recommendations before implementation.
